issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a male civilian-in-war-zone trauma profile, sexual objectification as a central trigger is not impossible, but in combination with the rest of the profile it lacks support from memory, threat, and appraisal items. The other items consistently describe war-related threat, distrust, flashbacks, and sensory trauma memory rather than sexualized threat, making this trigger hard to integrate into the same trauma presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding as a trigger is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected items. No memory, threat, or appraisal items reference water, drowning, environmental disaster, or any related theme. Given the otherwise interpersonal/war-threat profile, this trigger appears disconnected from the formulation.

issues.item: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the indexed trauma type. For a civilian in a war zone, water/flooding and alcohol smell are hard to reconcile with the threat, memory, and appraisal items unless there is some specific unreported trauma context linking them. The rest of the profile centers on generalized danger, distrust, flashbacks, and sensory recall, but these two triggers imply a different situational pattern that is not otherwise represented.

The maladaptive strategy set is partly disconnected from the rest of the formulation. Drug use is plausible as a broad coping strategy, but excessive exercise and concealing clothing suggest body-focused avoidance or managing visibility/safety in a specific way that is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items presented. Given the strong Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies and Threat → Maladaptive Strategies links, these strategies should plausibly follow from the reported triggers and threat beliefs, but these two items do not clearly do so.

vignette: Arjun stood in the market square when the ground shattered beneath him, the concrete dust and burning oil clinging to his clothes. What he remembers most clearly is not a single narrative but a series of sharp, unblinking frames: the sudden impact, the man in the grey coat falling forward, the acrid bite of fuel mixing with the familiar tang of his own sweat. Even now, Arjun can close his eyes and smell it again—the same sharp, oily scent that floods his throat when the memory surfaces. He knows exactly what happened to him that afternoon, yet when a colleague tries to coax the story from him, his tongue remains heavy, unable to find words to bridge the gap between knowing and speaking. The images stay sharp, locked behind his ribs, his memories of the frightening event clear and detailed, as if the event never fully left his peripheral vision. Returning to his life as a diplomat in Washington, Arjun learned to navigate a world that felt suddenly porous. He had come to believe that safety was a promise others made lightly, and even when his fiancée assured him the streets were secure, he found it impossible to believe it. A car backfiring down K Street sent his shoulders rising before his mind could register the sound; the sharp crack carried him instantly back to the square, his body bracing as if the stressful experience were actually happening again. What frightened him most was the smell of alcohol on a stranger’s breath or the faint clink of a glass in a diplomatic lobby, which would stir that same scent from the past and tighten his chest. Strangers approaching him in ordinary moments—a courier reaching for a signature, a colleague stepping too close in an elevator—made him feel threatened, as though their proximity carried a quiet weight. He had lost faith in the steady rhythm of daily life, certain that something about him had drawn the violence down, as though his very presence had made the event inevitable. To manage the mounting pressure, Arjun developed quiet routines that became his daily architecture. He began wearing concealing clothing to avoid being noticed in crowded embassy halls and official cars, the layered wool and structured collars creating a quiet boundary around his shoulders. When the memories grew loud, he pushed himself to exercise excessively, running until his breath steadied and his mind quieted. He repeated this with a kind of mechanical insistence, lacing his shoes each morning without fail. When physical exhaustion alone could not still the noise, he began taking drugs, letting the soft chemistry wash over him until the edges of the room softened again. These habits sat side by side in his days, each offering a different kind of shelter as the months passed, without one replacing the other. Now twenty-four, Arjun works in the diplomatic corps, where his office windows face a busy thoroughfare and his schedule demands constant interaction. He feels emotionally vulnerable in the open glass corridors of the embassy, where the hum of voices and the cadence of footsteps remind him of the square. He has a future on paper, but he has lost faith in its promise. He sits in his apartment some evenings, listening to his partner laugh in the other room, yet he is certain that the ground could still give way. He knows the world is physically safe, but he cannot trust the feeling of it. What brought him to seek help was not a single breaking point, but the slow accumulation of these quiet moments: the way he now counts exits in every building, the way he flinches when a door closes too sharply, the way he watches strangers approach his desk with a guarded stillness. He hopes someone might help him untangle the knot between what he knows and what he feels, though he carries a quiet hopelessness, certain he has no future unless he can quiet the watchfulness that keeps him standing at attention.
